articles.text: The Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) presented a check for $4,039,957 to Piedmont School District during a school board meeting on Wednesday, September 25. This substantial grant represents a year’s worth of dedicated fundraising by PEF members and demonstrates the community’s unwavering support for local education. The funds were raised through the annual Giving Campaign, Spring Fling, Harvest Festival, Dress Best for Less, business sponsorships, a the PEF endowment fund, and generous bequest from Pamela Wells Rafanelli. A former Piedmont resident and teacher at Havens and Beach schools, Rafanelli left a legacy gift to support professional development opportunities for Piedmont educators. PEF raised $321,660 through last year’s Spring Fling and Harvest Festival, which is being allocated to fund critical projects such as classroom technology, decodable books for the phonics curriculum, and initiatives to promote a positive playground culture at Beach, Havens, and Wildwood schools. articles.text: Editor: Summer 2024 was Earth’s hottest on record. It’s October. Still hot. Heed Mark Gongloff’s warning: “Global warming has arrived and we’re not ready.” All around us, our East Bay Regional Parks are under threat from wildfires, disease, drought, sea level rise, recklessness, and growing pains. With more than 100,000 acres of public land to protect, we need Lynda Deschambault’s depth of knowledge, tenacity and experience to respond to the climate urgency of now. Lynda will provide solid direction on Day 1. Lynda is the ONLY candidate with a 37-year career as an environmental scientist, 19-years at the U.S.EPA, 5+ years as Parks Commissioner, experience managing multi-million dollar budgets and programs, and crafting sound environmental policy. We need a trusted resource, tireless advocate and respected partner among local climate leaders, park staff, tribes and underserved communities. Elect Lynda Deschambault for East Bay Regional Park Board. –Renee Zeimer

articles.text: Editor: In 2013 the School District replaced its formerly progressive support tax with a single flat rate tax. Changing to a regressive flat tax resulted in 76% of Piedmont homeowners paying 6% to 21% more for those on parcels less than 10,000 square feet. Owners of large parcels, commercial properties and multi-unit buildings saw reductions of 7% to 80%. In 2019 the District partially corrected the regressive tax by adding a supplemental progressive per square foot of building tax. However 80% of the support tax structure remains a regressive flat rate tax. The better solution in 2019 would have been to have a single per square foot of building tax resulting in a 100% progressive tax structure. Several large local districts have gone to this model and their tax burden pales in comparison to Piedmont’s. articles.text: Piedmont Community Church will host a free showing in October of the documentary, Join or Die. Directed by Pete and Rebecca Davis, the film explains the benefits of joining a club or an organization. The screening will be at Piedmont Church, 400 Highland Avenue at 7 p.m. on Friday, October 25. “At a time when American society is more and more fractured – and our politics are increasingly fractious – the need for people to get together with others in face-to-face groups has never been stronger,” the church wrote in a press release. The film follows the journey of social scientist Robert Putnam, whose groundbreaking research, Bowling Alone: The Collapse and Revival of American Community, examines America’s decades-long decline in community connections. For more information contact Rev. Don Ashburn at Don@ PiedmontChurch.org.
articles.title: Community Church to host film screening in October.

articles.text: Piedmont is hosting its first ever Adult Recreation Expo this coming November, and the city is currently encouraging local organizations to attend. The Expo will take place on Sunday, November 17, from 2:00 to 4:30 p.m. at the Veterans Memorial Building. 401 Highland Avenue. Its goal is to help publicize adult recreational activities available to residents. Current participants include Piedmont Adult School, Piedmont Center for the Arts, League of Women Voters, and Piedmont Recreation Department. To sign up and for more information e-mail AdultRecreationExpo@piedmont.ca.gov. There is no cost. Organizers will be provided with tables and chairs at the event. The Expo was conceived by members of the Recreation Commission and is the result of a survey that was conducted. The deadline to register is October 18.
articles.title: Adult Recreation Expo deadline for signups is Oct. 18

articles.text: It seems that part of the rules for being a home beer brewer are that when naming your beer there are no rules. Looking at the names of some of the past year’s Artisanal Beer Festival names, one could conclude that coming up with a clever name for one’s beer is as important as the beer itself. Some of last year’s entrants included Stub Your Toein-the-Dark Ale, Cognitive Dissonance, Paul the Pilsner and the still mysterious Oaxacan Green Corn Saison. Jon Rhodin, a brewer for eight years, will present a double IPA named Ah, Bitter Dregs. You know it must be good with a name like that. Reyes will present a Mate Stout, a Passion Blonde and a Potato Saison. Patrons will need to taste all three to know what styles they represent. Trevor Fleshman, whose prior beers have leaned towards the exploratory side, this year presents Nipple Confusion, a single batch American IPA, one half containing 5% lactose, and the other half an unadulterated American IPA. Patrons will be challenged to pick which is which. Piedmont native Jessica Falarski Cross, once Trevor’s babysitter, is back for her second year. She and husband Kevin have created an anchor steam beer called California Common, which it certainly won’t be. Carter Dunlap, PCA board member, a home brewer, and the event organizer, plans to play it safe with Fifth Generation Cali, an American Red Ale with a West Coast twist and a nod to his California heritage. While most of the brewers have taken part before, this year Piedmont resident Michael Fodor a craft brewer for 20 years makes his debut at the festival. His entrant rounds out this year’s beers with a nod to P-town with his Dracena Haze, a West Coast Hazy Pale Ale made with hops harvested believe it or not near Dracena Park. articles.text: Staff photo Gary Randolph, 31, joined the Piedmont Fire Department as a paramedic in January and became a certified firefighter in July. When Gary Randolph was forced to evacuate his new home in Healdsburg with his wife during the 2019 Kincaid Fire, he remembered feeling completely helpless. Randolph, 31, had just moved into the house three months prior to the blaze, and while he was staying with relatives in the Sacramento area after the fire, he had an epiphany: He realized that he wanted to do whatever he could to fight a feeling of powerlessness in the face of disaster. “It was honestly right then and there I realized, ‘You know what? This is something that I want to do. I want to get into firefighting. I want to be able to help,’” Randolph said. Randolph said he took that inspiration and started asking associates who worked as firefighters what he could do to break into the service. That’s when he learned of the vast need for paramedics. “Every department, especially in California, is really looking for paramedics. That’s kind of the standard now,” Randolph said. “So in January 2020 I took my first EMT class, I got my certification and went straight from EMT into paramedic school.” He initially worked as a reserve firefighter in Healdsburg and as a paramedic with a private ambulance company for a year before he made his way to the Piedmont Fire Department, where he landed a job as a paramedic in January 2024. In March, he and two other Piedmont recruits were sent to the Las Positas College Fire Academy to become firefighters. Randolph and his colleagues graduated from the fire academy in July this summer and are now full-fledged firefighters with the Piedmont Fire Department. In addition to his new certifications, Randolph welcomed his first child – a baby boy named Hayden – on September 5. Randolph and his wife and son reside in Healdsburg, where his family has lived for four generations. HEATING AND AIR CONDITIONING COMPANY

articles.text: Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) representatives spoke to the Piedmont School Board about overcrowded classrooms at the high school and middle school on September 25. Kate Waldron of Piedmont Middle School and high school teacher Mercedes Foster described the current conditions at their schools in a discussion at the last school board meeting. They want the board and the community to be aware of the impacts the budget cuts have made to schools this year. The duo read their reports in alternating fashion, which detailed where the cutbacks hit at the two schools. The teachers stood before the school board and reported large class size numbers in some classes. Waldron, a PMS Math teacher, stated that Compression Math for eighth graders has an average of 33 students, and sixth graders in advanced math classes have an average of 31 students. “This year in many departments and for many specific courses, 30 or more students in the room has become the norm at Piedmont Middle School,” Teachers tell the district that some Piedmont Middle and High School classes are too crowded. explained Waldron. Foster reported larger numbers in some classes at the high school that at times have created a need to crawl over desks to go to the restroom. Calculus classes have 34 or more students, and Statistics and AP Spanish have classes with 35 students. “Larger classes change the behavior of students. articles.text: Part 4 in a series All three school board candidates continue to participate in the Post’s weekly questions posed to candidates for public office. One question was sent out on Thursday with a request to limit answers to 200 words. School Board, 4-year terms 3 open seats; 3 candidates Week 4 Question Please give an example of something you think is an underutilized resource for Piedmont students. Explain how it could benefit them. SUSY STRUBLE, Candidate PUSD graduates and the broader Piedmont community are valuable yet underutilized resources. The District is starting to develop programs, such as the PUSD Alumni Network, that go beyond traditional career day discussions. As this network matures, I hope it will noy only help students in exploring career and continued learning paths but also in navigating the transition from Piedmont into the wider world. I’m especially excited to see how the Alumni Network can help our kids understand that there are many paths to fulfillment and how to build their own flexible, healthy scaffolding for success in an ever-changing world. Insight from peers on these points carries more weight than anything parents and teachers might say. MICHAEL MALIONE, Candidate I think the most underutilized resource for Piedmont students is the career-related expertise of the parents, families, and retirees who live here. The PHS College and Career Center is doing a much bigger program this year, and it would be great to have broader community involvement in Career Day. Though parents volunteer their time at the schools in a variety of ways, the district underutilizes this resource in projects that are more directly on point to a particular community member’s skills and experience. Having more community involvement and better-coordinated community involvement would go a long way. The district recently launched a Piedmont Alumni Network, and I fully support such efforts. Further development to include parents and a volunteering aspect would continue the support of long-time parent volunteers, strengthen community in Piedmont, and most importantly, help PUSD students make better decisions in their preparations for life after graduation. MAX ROMAN, Candidate I think an underutilized resource for Piedmont students is the community. There are a lot of people who are experts in all sorts of fields who live here, and I think it would be terrific if there was some kind of program to connect students with experts in whatever they are studying in the community.

articles.text: Miranda Liu, a junior at Piedmont High School, participated in the Global Asian Moon Festival & Creator Summit on September 20 in Los Angeles. Liu was a part of a team of high school students that presented their short documentary “Crisis in Alviso,” which was featured at the event. The documentary cues in on environmental justice issues that have arisen in the northern San Jose district of Alviso, which lies on the southern shores of the Bay. Alviso is a small community where Hispanics and Asians make up nearly 75% of its population. Alviso was once a thriving port city shipping goods and produce to San Francisco, but Alviso has taken a concerning turn in recent decades. The Global Asian Moon Festival and Creator Summit showcased the creative power of Asia Americans, attracting cultural-minded audiences from around the world to celebrate the thriving of Asian cultural and creative industries. articles.text: This past July Troop 15 went to Camp Wente summer camp. There, Scouts checked off requirements, completed merit badges, and had tons of fun during the evening. Even the mosquitos and the deathly heat didn’t stop the Scouts from having a blast. The daily Scout schedule consisted of breakfast, merit badges, lunch, merit badges, dinner and evening activities. Scouts could choose from 85 different merit badges like archery, astronomy, emergency preparedness, kayaking, photography and many more. Theo said “I had fun doing the merit badges. I would go to Camp Wente again in a heart beat.” A merit badge many Scouts found very enjoyable was Riflery. The merit badge consisted of grouping three and five shots together five times each in the area of a quarter. Many found it exciting to learn how to handle a rifle and to see their progress in shooting. Scouts don’t need to shoot in consecutive rounds which makes the merit badge less stressful and you can complete it in the span of four days at the minimum. If the Scouts wanted an extra challenge they could try to get into, The Dime club. This is a club Scouts can only get it in if they group five shots together in the area of a dime. In addition to merit badges, Scouts had time to enjoy hanging out at the campsite, meeting Scouts from other Troops and trying to stay cool. articles.text: QB Lagios scores 5 touchdowns The Highlanders put together another dominant display on Friday, October 4 under the lights of Witter Field, blanking the visiting Dougherty Valley Wildcats 41-0. Piedmont’s football team improves its record to 4-1 and has outscored opponents 167-35 in its four-game winning streak. Piedmont put up 14 points in the first quarter and led 21-0 by halftime. Coach Jordan Seiden said it was their most complete performance this season and was glad to see his players remain hungry for more in the second half. “When the guys go into the locker room at halftime and they are disappointed, saying ‘We should be up more,’ that tells me that they know we can be even better. This was the most complete game we’ve played all season,” Seiden said. The Highlanders had 464 yards of total offense, with receiver Sam Shelby accounting for nearly half of it with 214 total receiving yards. Quarterback Markos Lagios accounted for four passing touchdowns and added another on the ground. “We expected a much more physical team and we just came out with that fire. Sam was doing his thing, he got me all those passing yards on little screens,” Lagios said. PHS now moves into the final stretch of the season with its five-game league schedule in the Western Alameda County Conference Mission Division. Piedmont received a promotion from the Shoreline Division last season after winning the title. It aims to win back-to-back league banners. “We have a big game next week in Hayward. I think this matchup has a lot of buzz around the league. After winning the Shoreline last year, we have some really tough competition in the Mission [Division]. Irvington is looking a lot better; Washington looks good. No one is going to hand us anything and we’re not sneaking up on anyone,” Seiden said. Game Recap After trading possession twice, Piedmont got on the board with Staff Photos Quarterback Markos Lagios pushes into the end zone for one of his five touchdowns against Dougherty Valley. 5:04 left in the first quarter with Shelby on 15 and 20-yard receptions, a 16-yard reception by Xavier Henderson, and a 20-yard touchdown run by Tommy Ashton. Miles Silver then recovered a chip kick over a Wildcats players’ head at the DVHS 23-yard line. Shelby helped convert a 4th-and-7 with a nine-yard reception to the 11, followed by Lagios tucking and running in a touchdown on a broken pass play with 2:11 left in the first. PHS’ next touchdown came on a seven-play drive, where Lagios took a carry 47 yards to the DV 22-yard line. The next play Lagios found Jack Meyjes on a crossing route underneath, running it into the end zone for his first varsity touchdown with 8:56 left in the second quarter. Piedmont put up 14 more points in the third quarter. Shelby turned a screen pass 65 yards down the sideline for a touchdown with 7:42 on the clock, then scored an 80-yard touchdown including a broken tackle with 4:02 left. After Miguel Long grabbed an interception, PHS scored in 13 plays on a 4th-and-Goal at the Wildcats’ three yard line, when Henderson caught a pass in the flat and ran it in easily, making it 41-0 after a missed extra point with 8:21 left in the game. Final stats: Lagios completed 20-25 passes for 279 yards and four touchdowns, to go along with 89 rushing yards and a touchdown. Shelby had 193 yards on nine receptions and two touchdowns, plus 21 rushing yards on two carries. Ashton had 68 rushing yards on nine carries and a touchdown. Henderson and Meyjes both had touchdown receptions. Defensively, Brandon Dicke had two tackles for loss; Henderson had one tackle for loss. Silver had a pass defense and fumble recovery. Long had an interception. NEXT UP Piedmont (4-1) heads to Hayward on Friday, October 11 for a 7:00 p.m. game. Sam Shelby had 193 receiving yards and touchdown runs of 80 and 65 yards. Jack Meyjes (14) celebrates a touchdown reception with Cash Elmquist.

articles.text: Photos by Lynne Wright Piedmont’s win over Lick-Wilmerding brings their record to 7-7, the school’s most since 2019. Piedmont High’s girls’ water polo continues its winning ways, this time with a 17-11 win over Lick-Wilmerding in San Francisco on Thursday, October 3. The victory improves the team’s record to 7-7, the most wins since 2019. The Highlanders have three matches left in the regular season. They have an opportunity to notch the most wins in a season since 2017, which went 10-13 and was led by the school’s AllTime leading goal-scorer, Annika Disney, who went on to play for Santa Clara. Thursday’s win marked another strong performance by Abigail Jacoby, who had three goals and five assists. Goalie Zoe Waitkus was critical with six saves and two assists on long throws. Game Recap Piedmont led 4-3 through the first quarter and continued a narrow one-goal advantage up 7-6 going into halftime. The Highlanders extended their lead to 13-8 in the third quarter and scored four while allowing three in the final going, 17-11. Lick-Wilmerding actually scored the game’s first goal just 51 seconds into the game, but Piedmont went up with three unanswered goals by Sydney Olson, Viviane Burke, and Julian Montes to lead 3-1 with 2:34 left in the first quarter. Lick came back to tie it at 3-3 with a minute left, but Rachel Young got PHS back on top by scoring just 20 seconds later on the ensuing possession. Olson got her second goal a minute and a half into the second quarter, while Abigail Jacoby made it 6-3 after Piedmont’s defense forced a change of possession with 5:06 left. After a Tigers goal, Jacoby scored again with 4:32 left in the half. Lick-Wilmerding added two goals prior to halftime, making it 7-6. I n t he t h i rd qu a r ter, Lick-Wilmerding tied the game at 7-7 with a goal with 5:44 remaining, but Burke and Celeste Dickason created a two-goal cushion with 3:16 on the clock. Piedmont added four straight goals to end the quarter up 13-8 by Esme Krumins, Jacoby, Olson, and Sonja ten Grotenhuis. PHS continued on the throttle in the fourth quarter, scoring after 20 seconds by #2 followed by Mari Pisani with 5:22 remaining in the game. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team suffered a tense 4-3 loss to Conference rivals, Berkeley, at the Berkeley Tennis Club on Thursday, October 3. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team traveled to CSU Monterey Bay for the 2024 Monterey Invitational on Friday and Saturday, October 4-5. Our defense dramatically improved as our communication got better,” said assistant coach John Savage. It was a big tournament for senior leader Elles Krieckhaus, who totaled 15 goals in the four matches. He scored five goals in Piedmont’s overtime win over Aptos and seven goals in the win over Morro Bay. “We are really happy with Elles’s progression this year, realizing he can be the best player in the water on both sides of the game; offense and defense,” Savage said. PHS maintained the two-goal advantage 10-8 through the third quarter, but Aptos tied the game at 12-12 with just 22 seconds left in the fourth quarter. After a scoreless first period of overtime, Piedmont’s Leo Hurwitz scored the game-winner with just four seconds left in the second OT. In the first, Piedmont’s Krieckhaus scored the opening two goals to put his school up 2-0 with 1:12 left but Aptos added one with 13 seconds left. PHS added another two within the first two minutes of the second quarter by Rylan Patty and Hurwitz, while Krieckhaus made it 5-2 with 3:47 on the clock. articles.text: Legendary jazz fusion guitarist Al Di Meola will play five shows at Yoshi’s in Oakland this weekend, Friday through Sunday, October 11-13. Meola is among the top guitarists of our time. His fascination with complex rhythmic syncopation combined with provocative lyrical melodies and sophisticated harmony has been at the heart of his music throughout a career that has spanned four decades. He has produced four gold albums and two platinum albums, with six million record sales worldwide and five German gold albums. His awards include an Honorary Doctorate Degree from Berklee College of Music, the Honorary Miles Davis Award presented by the Montreal Jazz Festival, a BBC Lifetime Achievement Award presented by Sir George Martin in 2008, Hungarian Foundation for Performing Arts Lyra Award and numerous Grammy awards and nominations and awards. Not only a guitar hero but a prolific composer, Di Meola has amassed over 30 albums as a leader while collaborating on a dozen others with the fusion supergroup Return to Forever Al Di Meola will play at Yoshi’s in Oakland this weekend, Friday through Sunday, October 11-13. (with Chick Corea, Stanley Clarke and Lenny White). The celebrated acoustic Guitar Trio features virtuoso John McLaughlin; and the Rite of Strings trio with bassist Clarke and violinist Jean-Luc Ponty. A pioneer of blending world music and jazz, going back to early Latin-tinged fusion outings like 1976’s Land of the Midnight Sun, 1977’s Elegant Gypsy and 1978’s Casino, the guitar great continues to explore the rich influence of flamenco, tango, Middle Eastern, Brazilian and African music with his World Sinfonia, a global group that he formed in 1991. Tickets for the evening shows ($49-$99) are available at yoshis. com/events/buy-tickets.

articles.text: This Sunday will mark the last show of the dazzling musical The Prom, which kicked off the 2024-2025 season of Berkeley Playhouse. Set in small-town Indiana, The Prom follows four eccentric Broadway stars who swoop into a conservative community to boost their careers by championing a high school student’s right to bring her girlfriend to the prom. The musical premiered on Broadway in 2018 and earned seven Tony Award nominations. It was followed by a movie (featuring Meryl Streep and Nicole Kidman), a national tour, and productions in top regional theaters across the U.S. Now, for a few more days at the Julia Morgan Theater, audiences can experience this hit Broadway musical, renowned for its infectious energy and poignant storytelling. Co-director Christina Lazo expressed the impor tance of presenting the musical in today’s world: “There have been instances over the years across the country of parents pulling their students from high school productions and local theaters canceling their shows due to the material. We have to do this show and keep doing shows like this. I can’t wait for audiences to see the sparkle and the beauty of the world within The Prom.” “This is a special show that is so much fun with tons of dancing and big numbers, but that is also full of heartfelt moments and important themes of acceptance,” added co-director McGrath. “The best part of the story is at the end where everyone gets to celebrate their truest selves.” For tickets ($19–$55) or more information, the public may call 845-8542 x351 or visit berkeleyplayhouse.org. Group rates are available for 10 or more people. All performances will take place at Berkeley Playhouse, 2640 College Avenue in Berkeley. articles.text: From now through February 18, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art presents Get in the Game: Sports, Art, Culture, exploring the place of sports in our society. Get in the Game, together with six sports-related companion exhibitions, will be the museum’s most expansive presentation dedicated to any one subject to date, covering over 15,000 square feet with over 200 compelling artworks and design objects by over 70 artists. Viewers will discover the sense of community found in depictions including pickup basketball games, minor league baseball teams, neighborhood swimming clubs and surfing groups. Audiences will also encounter artists and designers inspired by athletes promoting conversations about gender and race, as well as artworks responding to the remarkable achievements of sports figures such as Muhammad Ali, Michael Jordan, Diana Nyad and Venus Williams. Woven throughout Get in the Game are stunning works of contemporary art and design, interactive installations and historical videos that reconsider political and cultural issues through the lens of athleticism, competition and play. “Get in the Game explores the confluence of culture and sports and the many ways in which they influence each other. The exhibition creates space for dynamic conversations about identity, physicality, passion, ambition, and resilience”, said Christopher Bedford, SFMOMA Director. Upending our expectations of museums and games, viewers will be able to play interactive artworks by contemporary artists: Maurizio Cattelan’s 22-person foosball table, Stadium (1991), and Gabriel Orozco’s Ping Pond Table (1998), a four-way pingpong table with a square pool in place of a net. Get in the Game features dozens of innovative designs for sports gear, gaming and fashion, including Formula One race car steering wheels, a 2022 ensemble from Virgil Abloh’s final Louis Vuitton collection, Michael Johnson’s gold running shoes, Nike’s original Air Jordan basketball shoes, and the technological advances of surfboards, tennis racquets and football helmets. Reflecting the evolving field of play, the exhibition also integrates designs from more recent years, such as the Cheetah Xceed prosthetic running leg, developed by biomedical engineer Van Phillips an amputee, and the Refugee Nation Flag, designed by artist Yara Said, a Syrian refugee now in Amsterdam. SFMOMA (151 Third Street in San Francisco, is open 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Friday through Tuesday, and 12 p.m. through 8 p.m. on Thursdays. Tickets ($30 general, $25 senior, $23 student, free 18 and younger) are available at sfmoma.org/visit.

articles.text: The de Young Museum in San Francisco will open the first major U.S. retrospective of Tamara de Lempicka this Sunday, with over 150 works on display through February 9. Through her glamorous lifestyle, artist Tamara de Lempicka (1894-1980) has become synonymous with the carefree spirit and opulence of the 1920s. Her paintings, combining a classical figural style with the modern energy of avant-garde, have cemented Lempicka as one of Art Deco’s defining painters. Retrospective Tamara de Lempicka, the first exhibition in the United States dedicated to the artist’s full oeuvre, will reveal a new perspective on her life and art practice. In addition to her celebrated portraits, the exhibit will include a number of rarely seen drawings, experimental still lifes from Lempicka’s early Parisian years and melancholic domestic interiors, as well as a selection of Art Deco objects, sculptures and dresses from the museum’s collection. The exhibition is co-curated by Furio Rinaldi and Gioia Mori. “Considering San Francisco’s history as a great Art Deco capital of the world, the exhibition – aptly presented in close proximity to landmarks of the period such as the Golden Gate Bridge and Coit Tower – adds to our understanding not only of Lempicka’s work specifically, but also this influential art and design period at large,” said Thomas P. Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “The combination of varied artistic influences in Europe during the interwar period constitute the ingredients for Lempicka’s unique visual language, a captivating and unique blend of classicism and modernism,” said Gioia Mori, exhibition co-curator. Tamara de Lempicka unfolds chronologically in four major chapters that mark the stages in the artist’s life through her changing identity: “Tamara Rosa Hurwitz” (her birth name), “Monsieur Łempitzky,” “Tamara de Lempicka,” and “Baroness Kuffner.” These sections include poignant and experimental still lifes from Lempicka’s early Parisian years, figural works inspired by the Russian avant-gardes and Cubist inspirations from her painting teacher André Lhote, while highlighting Lempicka’s appreciation for the work of Neoclassical painters of the 18th century like Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres. The de Young Museum (50 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive, San Francisco) is open from 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m., Tuesday through Sunday. Tickets ($20 adult, $17 senior, $11 student, free under 18) are available at: ticketing.famsf.org/ events. Tamara de Lempicka, Young Girl with Gloves, detail, 1930–1931. articles.text: This Sunday, October 13, the Piedmont Center for the Arts will host the first of three events in a new series, Japanese Internment Camps: Life, Art, and Music. This first event, “My Dad, the Activist,” starts at 4 p.m. and will feature Karen Korematsu, daughter of Oakland-born Fred Korematsu, who was arrested and convicted in Federal Court for resisting military orders to report for transfer to an internment camp in 1942. He appealed this conviction all the way to the Supreme Court, where it was overturned in 1983. Karen will share his father’s story and that of her family during the internment years, She will answer audience questions and take part in a meet-and-greet reception at the Center. The second event in the series, “Remembering, 80 Years Later,” will be held on Sunday, November 2 and feature Wendy Tokuda, a former Piedmont resident and award-winning former News Anchor at KPIX in San Francisco. She will share stories of her family’s time in the camps. Kimi Hill, the granddaughter of famed artist and interned UC Berkeley professor Chiura Obata, will share art produced in the camps, including her father’s. The third event, held on November 23, will feature a screening of Alternative Facts: The Lies of Executive Order 9066, a documentary by John Osaki about the false information and political influence which led to the World War II incarceration of Japanese-Americans. After the screening, Osaki will discuss the film with Piedmont resident Don Tamaki, the attorney instrumental in getting Fred Korematsu’s conviction vacated by the Federal District Court in 1983. articles.text: Miles Graber will present the Mila Trio in concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, October 25 at 7:30 p.m. The tiro includes flautist Martha Aarons, violinist Lev Polyakin, and Graber on piano. Advance tickets are $35 in advance and $40 at the door. (https://bpt.me/6465993). The combination of violin, flute, and piano is most unusual in chamber music. Although there are countless works for violin or flute with piano, there are only a handful of works for these three instruments together. In a concert with pianist Miles Graber and the Mila Trio, audience members will be treated to two lovely works for the trio, complemented by three pieces for the individual instruments with piano. The two very stylistically contrasting pieces are J.S. Bach’s Trio Sonata in G major BWV 1038, and “Five Pieces” Op. 56, by the Russian composer Cesar Cui (1835- 1918). Manuel de Falla composed the “Siete Canciones Populares Españolas” for soprano and piano in 1914. He subsequently arranged the set (minus the second song) for violin and piano for the violinist Paul Kochanski, and it is this arrangement that will be performed. Pyotr Tchaikovsky wrote “Meditation” in 1878, originally as the slow movement of his violin concerto. He subsequently transcribed it for violin and piano as the first movement in a set called “Souvenir d’un Lieu Cher,” the “dear place” being the estate of his patroness Nadezhda von Meck. The piece for flute solo and piano is the beloved sonata of Francis Poulenc (1899-1963), a late work written in 1957 and debuted by Jean-Pierre Rampal with the composer at the piano.

articles.text: San Francisco’s longest-running literary festival returns to celebrate its 25th year with over 120 literary events throughout the city in just over two weeks. Events running from Thursday, October 10 to Saturday, October 26 include reading series, publisher talks and bookstore exhibitions catering to all ages and tastes. It’s the best single event in the Bay for literature lovers to get a sense of what’s happening locally; nearly 80% of last year’s 570 featured authors, for instance, called the Bay home. A few of this year’s featured authors include Maxine Hong Kingston, Chinese-American novelist and National Book Award for Nonfiction winner; Daniel Handler, alias Lemony Snicket and author of many children’s books including the A Series of Unfortunate Events series; novelist Rachel Kushner, a Guggenheim Foundation Fellow, Prix Médicis winner and the recipient of an American Academy of Arts and Letters award; best-selling author and award-winning neuroscientist Daniel Levitin; and stand-up comedian, essayist and Academy Award-nominated actress Jenny Slate. One highlight of this year’s festival is the Booksellers Ball on October 10 from 7 to 10 p.m. at Club Fugazi in North Beach (678 Green Street), with beer, wine and delicious food; entertainment including music and dancing; and a reading nook with surprise exhibitions. Tickets range from $75 to $100, and all proceeds will support the Litquake Foundation. Another keystone of the festival is Kidquake, consisting of two days of citywide in-person and virtual talks and meet-and-greets with a diverse array of children’s book creators from October 10 to October 11, alongside activities run by the Bay’s top interactive educators. Each student leaves the in-person events with a new book, and teachers receive a bag of books and other goodies for their classrooms. Kidquake is completely free, and serves thousands of Bay Area K-5 public school students every year. A schedule of both days is available at litquake.org/ kidquake. Book lovers are urged to not miss the Litquake Book Fair on Saturday, October 19 from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. at Yerba Buena Gardens (750 Howard Street). A curated spread of 18 small presses and literary magazines will have local literature on offer throughout a day of poetry readings and music. Litquake will culminate with one of the Bay’s most anticipated literary nights of the year, Lit Crawl: a massive, one-night literary pub crawl through San Francisco’s Mission District that will bring together over 250 authors and an estimated 5,000 fans for the world’s largest free pop-up literary event. Since its founding in 2004, Lit Crawl has cultivated a unique, resonant tone: smart and silly, worldly and wacky, with events presented in venues usual to literary readings (bars, cafes, galleries and bookstores) and unusual (police stations, tattoo parlors, barbershops and laundromats). Many Litquake events are free and open to attend, although RSVP and ticket requirements vary. A full schedule of the festival, with descriptions of all featured authors, is available at litquake.org.

articles.text: Noomi Rapace and Michael Nyquist star in The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo who should have cared for her. The result is a young woman who is profoundly mistrustful of all authority. There is likely not enough time or therapy to unravel Lisbeth, if she would, even for a moment, consider trying. The question then is: can the first of what will be three films capture the essence of Salander while detailing a complex serial-murder mystery? All in 2 ½ hours. The answer is yes. Filmed in Northern Sweden, the movie has a brooding, stark feel to it, much of it shot in winter, involving a 40-something journalist, Mikael Blomkvist (Michael Nyquist). He is hired by an aging industrialist to find the person who, he assumes, murdered his 16-year-old niece some 40 years before. In every way it is a cold case, a case that at first blush seems intricate and unsolvable. The police tried. Yet, when Lisbeth is recruited, pieces to the jigsaw begin to come together revealing not just one murder, but a series of women, killed horribly and then mutilated, suggesting a terrible pathology at work. The film is wonderfully shot by cinematographer Eric Kress, and well acted by the Swedish ensemble. Of course, the crucial challenge was who to cast as Salander. Rapace is perfect, a slip of a woman, who conveys with her silence and anger and intelligence, her vulnerability while remaining well-defended, with an emotional carapace ever intact. Regarding the book and the film, there’s an inherent conundrum: if you read the book first, then the film will be eminently interesting, though without surprise. The twists at the end will be anticipated. But to watch the film before reading the book will reveal the ending and take some of the punch out of the story. The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo is a wonderful murder mystery, a classic whodunit, and the perpetrator is not disclosed until necessary making for a ripper of a climax as well as a very nice surprise embedded in the denouement. The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo. Directed by Niels Arden Oplev, In Swedish with subtitles. Starring Noomi Rapace, Michael Nyquist and Lena Endre. 2 hrs, 32 min. Rated R. Streaming on Prime. Released in 2010.

articles.text: Woody Allen is a serial monogamist when it comes to world-class cities. He fell in love with New York, then London, briefly Spain, and now Paris. Ah, Paris. Allen caresses its wide boulevards and avenues, reveals skylines under a startling blue sky, captures the wide sidewalks, damp from rain, the busy outdoor cafes, the lovely restaurants and grand lobbies of hotels. From the first frame of Midnight in Paris, photographed by the gifted cinematographer, Darius Khondji, Allen gives the city of lights a lingering embrace that ripples throughout the film. Gil Pender (Owen Wilson) and his fiancée, Inez (Rachel McAdams), have joined her parents (Kurt Fuller and Mimi Kennedy) in Paris. Gil is enchanted by the city, wants to walk the streets in the rain, especially the rain, and waxes nostalgic about what he believes were the glorious 1920s, the golden age when writers and artists, known as the Lost Generation, took up residence. A screenwriter in Hollywood, Gil tells Inez that he would love to move to Paris, find inspiration, and work on his novel – his protagonist owns a nostalgia shop filled with memorabilia. Inez, a lovely, mercenary young thing with the heart of a philistine, doesn’t grasp anything that Gil is attempting to convey, nor do her suspicious, judgmental parents. So instead of spending time with Inez clubbing, he wanders the streets of Paris into the midnight hours. And it’s on one such late night peregrination, feeling lost, literally and figuratively, that a classic Peugeot town car stops and a couple, formally dressed, insist that he join them. Her backstory is a series of tragedies and failures by those Noomi Rapace and Michael Nyquist star in The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo who should have cared for her. The result is a young woman who is profoundly mistrustful of all authority. There is likely not enough time or therapy to unravel Lisbeth, if she would, even for a moment, consider trying. The question then is: can the first of what will be three films capture the essence of Salander while detailing a complex serial-murder mystery? All in 2 ½ hours. The answer is yes. Filmed in Northern Sweden, the movie has a brooding, stark feel to it, much of it shot in winter, involving a 40-something journalist, Mikael Blomkvist (Michael Nyquist). He is hired by an aging industrialist to find the person who, he assumes, murdered his 16-year-old niece some 40 years before. In every way it is a cold case, a case that at first blush seems intricate and unsolvable. The police tried. Yet, when Lisbeth is recruited, pieces to the jigsaw begin to come together revealing not just one murder, but a series of women, killed horribly and then mutilated, suggesting a terrible pathology at work. The film is wonderfully shot by cinematographer Eric Kress, and well acted by the Swedish ensemble. Of course, the crucial challenge was who to cast as Salander. Rapace is perfect, a slip of a woman, who conveys with her silence and anger and intelligence, her vulnerability while remaining well-defended, with an emotional carapace ever intact. Regarding the book and the film, there’s an inherent conundrum: if you read the book first, then the film will be eminently interesting, though without surprise. The twists at the end will be anticipated. But to watch the film before reading the book will reveal the ending and take some of the punch out of the story. The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo is a wonderful murder mystery, a classic whodunit, and the perpetrator is not disclosed until necessary making for a ripper of a climax as well as a very nice surprise embedded in the denouement. My Neighbor Totoro, an early work, is no exception. Actually, if you, the reader, have yet to sample one of films, and are always in the hunt for a compelling G-rated film for the young ones, Totoro would be a solid beginning. The story is absent rough edged villains. There is no conflict, and it is told from the point of view of two young sisters, Mei and Satsuki (Dakota Fanning and Elle Fanning). It is, as well, an extraordinary co-mingling of fantasy and reality, which defines the essence of childhood. A scene from Hayao Miyazaki’s Princess Mononoke Princess Mononoke is an epic story set in Medieval Japan during its iron-age period. A world order, so to speak, is in transition: the balance between the forces of nature and those trying to bend the natural world to their own purpose is in conflict. However, animator/ director/ and storyteller Miyazaki often blurs the lines between good and evil, creating a sense of compelling ambiguity in this narrative wherein humans, forest animals and nature gods struggle for their share of the changing order. The film opens with a watchtower guard spotting “something wrong in the forest.” Out of this disturbance leaps a remarkable creature, a kind of boar-monster with flesh made of writhing snakes. It attacks the villagers and riding to their defense comes Ashitaka (Billy Crudup), a young prince of an isolated people. He is encouraged to begin a journey west and try and discover what the source of the disturbance is. He rides a Yakkuru, a beast that is part horse, part antelope and part goat. articles.text: The Piedmont Post is presenting one month of reviews of films by celebrated Japanese animation director Hayao Miyazaki. As a writer, director, and animator he is one of the most revered filmmakers in Japan, and worldwide. His award-wining animated films have been embraced by audiences that have found his beautifully detailed hand-drawn visuals and thematic storytelling compelling. As well, his protagonists are often strong young girls or resilient young women. Miyazaki co-founded the now iconic Studio Ghibli in 1985. In 2012 he was named a Person of Cultural Merit by Japan for his outstanding cultural contributions. He received an Academy Honorary Award for his impact on animation and cinema in 2014. His work continues to serve as an inspiration for countless animators, directors and writers. This week’s reviews are: Princess Mononoke (1997) and My Neighbor Totoro (1988).

Part 1 In my 23 years of being a wine journalist I have traveled to many countries and several continents to visit the major wine regions of the world. One region I had missed was the wine growing region of Washington state. I have had many fine wines from Walla Walla and knew their reputation was soaring, but I had yet to visit. This past month that omission was corrected as I journeyed there with my good friends Wine. com founder Mike Osborn and winemaker Kent Rasmussen. Flying into Pasco and the Tri-Cities area and driving east one hour to Walla Walla you pass through vast open spaces of scrubland interlaced with wheat fields. Part of the journey included the Columbia River with its dramatic gorges and beautiful scenery. Walla Walla (“place of many waters” in the Nez Pearce language) is a green oasis of treelined streets, verdant parks and tidy wooden houses. With a population of around 34,000 it seems like a charming, livable city that would be a great place to raise a family. In the last 20 years Walla Walla has morphed from quiet, overlooked wheat town to a vibrant wine capital of Washington state. Leonetti, the area’s first winery, was started in 1973 and for years there were just a handful of wineries in the area. There are now over 120 wineries, and the main street is packed with tasting rooms promoting their wines. There are charming Bed and Breakfast places and Air B&B and trendy restaurants galore. In the early days of the wine industry most of the attention was focused on growing Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon. While those wines continue to thrive, the rising star is the Syrah grape, and the region has been winning major accolades for those wines. Ferguson is L’Ecole No. 41’s flagship Bordeaux Blend.

The acidity is woven into every fiber of the fruit, carrying it through the long finish. By Pierre DuMont Part 1 In my 23 years of being a wine journalist I have traveled to many countries and several continents to visit the major wine regions of the world. One region I had missed was the wine growing region of Washington state. I have had many fine wines from Walla Walla and knew their reputation was soaring, but I had yet to visit. This past month that omission was corrected as I journeyed there with my good friends Wine. com founder Mike Osborn and winemaker Kent Rasmussen. Flying into Pasco and the Tri-Cities area and driving east one hour to Walla Walla you pass through vast open spaces of scrubland interlaced with wheat fields. Part of the journey included the Columbia River with its dramatic gorges and beautiful scenery. Walla Walla (“place of many waters” in the Nez Pearce language) is a green oasis of treelined streets, verdant parks and tidy wooden houses. With a population of around 34,000 it seems like a charming, livable city that would be a great place to raise a family. In the last 20 years Walla Walla has morphed from quiet, overlooked wheat town to a vibrant wine capital of Washington state. Leonetti, the area’s first winery, was started in 1973 and for years there were just a handful of wineries in the area. There are now over 120 wineries, and the main street is packed with tasting rooms promoting their wines. There are charming Bed and Breakfast places and Air B&B and trendy restaurants galore. In the early days of the wine industry most of the attention was focused on growing Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon. While those wines continue to thrive, the rising star is the Syrah grape, and the region has been winning major accolades for those wines. L’Ecole 41 Winery tasting rooms don’t get much cuter than this. It is housed in the old Frenchtown school just outside of Walla Walla. Purchased in 1983 it was the third winery in Walla Walla. This third-generation owned winery is now run by Marty and Megan Clubb. Marty, an expert on the geography of the Walla Walla growing region, gave us a fascinating tour of their vineyards and topography. The L’Ecole 41 wines are widely available with national and international distribution. (see lecole.com) • 2022 L’Ecole No.41 Semillon Stillwater Creek, $25 This winery has long been famous for its Semillon, a grape that is in my mind underappreciated and overlooked. Like the excellent examples from Australia’s Hunter Valley, this concentrated wine shows green apple, sage, preserved citrus and lemongrass. The acidity is woven into every fiber of the fruit, carrying it through the long finish. Will benefit from time in the cellar. • 2022 L’Ecole No. 41 Luminesce Seven Hills Vineyard, $28 A blend of 60% Semillon and 40% Sauvignon Blanc this wine reminds me of a fine Bordeaux blanc. It does see a percentage of new French oak which gives a sweet vanilla note to the nose. In the mouth you get peaches, apricots and pears. It has a nice round mouthfeel and a savory finish. Perfect partner to roast chicken. The L’Ecole No. 41 tasting room is an old historic schoolhouse. • 2021 L’Ecole No. 41 Syrah Seven Hills Vineyard, $42 The wine is opaque purple-magenta in the glass. It opens with a full-throttle nose of dark fruit aromas, dried herbs black pepper and vanilla. The palate is medium bodied with a seamless, svelte texture transitioning to a savory finish with soft tannins and meaty undertones. • 2021 L’Ecole No. 41 Merlot Estate, $42 The Estate Merlot leads with brambly mintiness, cocoa and dark chocolate plum and herbs. This is a classy wine. It nails the traditional Merlot characters and is impeccably balanced and layered ending with soft inviting tannins. • 2021 L’Ecole No. 41 Apogee, $60 Hailing from the famous Pepperbridge Vineyard, this Bordeaux blend opens with blackcurrants leather and fresh herb aromas. The palate combines sturdy, dusty dark fruit flavors with admirable finesse. It shows judicious use of new wood which gives complexity and sturdiness. The wine should develop beautifully for two decades in the cellar. • 2021 L’Ecole No. 41 Ferguson Estate, $75 This Bordeaux blend uses all five of the traditional Bordeaux varietals in the mix. It offers up aromas of wild berries, cassis, licorice, rose petals and earth followed by a medium to full-bodied velvety and seamless palate, its structuring tannins hidden in an ample core of lively, succulent fruit. A dead ringer for a top growth Bordeaux. K Vintners One of the highlights of our Walla Walla trip was the invitation to have dinner at the home of Charles Smith, founder of K Vintners. Smith lives in a historic wooden house tucked beside a creek behind one of his vineyards. Over Smith’s dinner of fresh oysters, pasta and swordfish steaks we had a chance to sample some of his old K Syrahs and get to know this iconic Washington wine figure. Smith became interested in wine while working in restaurants at age 19. After veering off-track to spend a decade touring Europe as a rock band manager in Denmark, he returned to the U.S. to open a wine shop on Ferguson is L’Ecole No. 41’s flagship Bordeaux Blend. K Vintners in Washington is King of Syrah. Bainbridge Island by Seattle. But Charles’ real calling was not selling wine but making it. He made his way to Walla Walla where he got the opportunity to jump into the business. With almost nothing in his pockets, he found a way to produce his first vintage – 330 cases of 1999 K Syrah in 1999. In the two decades since he has become a celebrity winemaker. He developed (and later sold) iconic brands like House Wine and Kung Fu Girl Riesling. But the heart of Smith’s portfolio remains the Rhone-inspired K Vintners label. (His entire portfolio can be found at Houseofsmith. com.) • 2021 K Vintners M.C.K. (Motor City Kitty), $40 (Best Value) This is 100% Syrah from the Boushey Vineyard in Yakima Valley. The MCK is youthfully dense with aromas of blackcurrant, leather, charcuterie and coffee. The full-bodied palate has a round mouthfeel and mouthwatering acidity to enliven its concentrated, savory fruit and go with the long, lingering finish. This bargain priced Syrah is the best value of the lineup. See Wine Corner on page 31

pages.text: 26 Wednesday, October 9, 2024 Walking on Wednesday Exploring some new territory By Dick Carter Twenty-eight heat resistant members of the Walking on Wednesdays group gathered last Wednesday for a walk, though the forecast was for temperatures in the 90s. One seldom traveled Piedmont street the walkers hadn’t gotten to this year was activity leader Dick Carter’s Florada Avenue. Getting to it would let the walkers have a “fall colors” experience on Wildwood Avenue where its maple trees were almost-New England colorful. Additionally, the group could walk through Wildwood Gardens and check out the controversial vacant lot/house project on Wistaria Way. However, a walkthrough Wildwood Gardens would be incomplete without some history of Frank Colton Havens, the man responsible for it. The walkers went down Highland Avenue, turned up Wildwood Avenue, and stopped to enjoy the red leaves on the maple trees that line both sides of the block. A group photo was taken and some history from Gail Lombardi’s Piedmont Historical Society articles and Meghan Bennett’s History of Piedmont website was told. Frank C. Havens came to San Francisco from New York in 1866 and worked in banking, stocks, insurance, and investments. In 1895 he created the Oakland-based “Realty Syndicate” with F. M. “Borax” Smith. They became major real estate developers in the East Bay, particularly in Oakland, Berkeley, and Piedmont. The Syndicate accumulated at least 13,000 aces of valuable hilltop land that stretched from Mills College to North Berkeley. It built the Claremont Hotel in Berkeley and was also the parent company of the Key System transit company. Ken Hubbert provided some new information from the book Borax Pioneer about Smith. At some point before 1910, Smith and Havens came into conflict, for reasons unknown. One explanation was Smith joined in a water business that competed with a Havens business. Another was that Havens knew where Key System lines were going to be built and tipped off his family and friends to buy the land first at Smith’s expense. On December 9, 1910 it was made public that they had divided their interests, and sadly, after they had created so much together, never met or spoke again. Havens owned all the land from Crocker Avenue to Oakmont Avenue and Oak Road, and wanted to build an estate that he would call “Wildwood.” Havens’ mansion is at 101 Wildwood Gardens, which the walkers went to earlier this year. The group turned into Wildwood Gardens, passing two partially hidden pillars that marked the entrance to Havens’ estate. They walked up to Wistaria Way to a recently cleared lot. It was once part of a home that was donated to a local church and sold in 2022. The walkers were surprised to see work in progress. A large piece of equipment was down the hillside and drilling large holes for piers that will secure the home’s foundation. By chance, the landowner, Geoff Gibson, was there and explained he was dividing the lot into two parcels and constructing two new homes, one for his family, with an ADU alongside one. The neighbors have issues with it, but the project is moving forward. The walkers emerged on Woodland Way, then over to LaSalle Avenue and down to the little traveled Florada Avenue, the location of the Carters’ home. Further down the street is the Oakland/Piedmont city line where the street becomes Portal Avenue. That was as much Oakland exploration most walkers wanted on such a hot day, But some went on to see an Oakland house with a wonderful cactus garden. By chance the owner was outside and told them about his 15-year gardening project. The return to the city center was on LaSalle, Muir, and Crocker Avenues, Wildwood and Sheridan Avenues. articles.text: Piedmont’s third largest community event, the Harvest Festival, had more going on than immediately met the eye on September 22. The Festival include an art exhibit each year at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. While the center sounds of Harvest Festival activities saturated the park, the Art Exhibition was a stand-out spectacle of local art talent. Long-time organizer of the exhibit Jane Reed gathered talented Piedmont artists to supply pieces for the show. Adult artists included Jon Schleuning, with some of his drawings, and Bonnie Bonner, aka Joanne Palamountain, displayed some of her more contemporary pieces including Undressing for Winter, a giclee print on canvas of an Aspen sapling. Many different mediums of art were on display, including 7th grader Evan Shim’s crocheted stuffed animals. Shim nearly sold all his pieces during the festival. Another 7th grader, Peter Zee, displayed his croqueted medieval knight’s chest armor. “I was especially proud to see my son have his work displayed this year. He worked on his piece completely by himself whenever he could find free time between soccer or robotics practice. We calculated that it took him 40 hours of work to finish his piece and he designed his own pattern. He also crafted the helmet on his own using cardboard, a glue gun, and paint,” said mom Tracie. “It takes a lot of early mornings or late nights to capture some of these moments, so I’m happy that others can see these too,” said photographer Tracie with Picture Happy Photos. “Some of those unique alignments of the sun or moon to famous Bay Area landmarks were captured from right here in Piedmont.” Art lovers chat with artists at the 2024 Harvest Festival’s Art Exhibit. Lorrel Plimier, Candidate Because we have so little commercial and mixed-use space in Piedmont, it’s important to be very intentional when it comes to permitting for businesses. We currently have 19 parcels in Piedmont zoned for commercial use and six of those contain a single-family home, which means they are not being used commercially. Businesses in Piedmont should meet the needs of our residents and foster community among our residents. It’s also very important to get community input when discussing changes to Piedmont’s by-right permitted commercial uses. The city conducted a survey of the community to gather input on what type of commercial use our community members favored for Piedmont. There was overwhelming support for a community gathering space. Liu prepared a presentation and spoke at the festival about the community of Alviso, that lives below sea level due to the history of excessive groundwater pumping for agricultural and residential uses. During the Gold Rush in the mid-19th century, large quantities of mercury were used in the mining process to extract gold from ore. This led to significant mercury contamination in the waterways leading into Alviso. Environmental problems continue as freshwater has been diverted into the Alviso wetlands, lowering critical salt levels, allowing invasive plants to infiltrate, squeezing out the native plants. The documentary introduces the community of Alviso, which also faces gentrification, the loss of affordable housing, and the erosion of the community’s cultural fabric in the wake of rapid urbanization in Silicon Valley.
